practice: Legume-based cover cropping between main crop cycles
summary: Sowing nitrogen-fixing cover crops (cowpea, horsegram, sunn hemp) in the fallow window instead of leaving soil bare.
mechanism: Living roots keep rhizosphere carbon flowing year-round and legume residues have a low C:N ratio, so they mineralise into stable organic matter rather than burning off. Continuous ground cover lowers soil surface temperature and evaporative loss, which raises microbial biomass; microbial biomass is the base of the soil food web that ground-nesting invertebrates and insectivorous birds depend on.

effects.magnitude: roughly 15-25% relative gain in the topsoil over 2-3 seasons
measurable reduction in evaporative loss from continuous cover
higher soil invertebrate and pollinator counts where flowering legumes are used

source: FAO, Conservation Agriculture and Soil Organic Carbon guidance; FAO/ITPS Status of the World's Soil Resources

practice: Alley-cropping agroforestry with nitrogen-fixing trees
summary: Planting rows of multipurpose trees (Gliricidia, Leucaena, Faidherbia) through cropland with the crop grown in the alleys.
mechanism: Deep tree roots pull water and nutrients from below the crop rooting zone, so the system uses rainfall that a sole crop would miss. Litterfall and root turnover add carbon at depth where it is more stable than surface residue. The tree rows act as permanent structural habitat inside an otherwise annual system, giving birds, bats and arboreal insects perch and nesting structure across the whole year.

effects.magnitude: commonly reported gains of 0.2-0.5 tC per hectare per year above sole cropping
bird and arthropod richness typically intermediate between sole crop and natural woodland
tree rows function as within-field corridors

source: IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU); FAO Advancing Agroforestry on the Policy Agenda

practice: Contour bunding and staggered trenches on sloping land
summary: Earthen bunds and trenches cut along the contour to slow runoff and force infiltration.
mechanism: Slowing overland flow increases residence time so water infiltrates rather than leaving the plot, which raises profile moisture and recharges shallow groundwater. Retained sediment also retains the organic fraction that would otherwise be the first thing lost to erosion. The wetted zone behind each bund becomes a refuge strip where moisture-dependent species persist through the dry season.

effects.magnitude: substantial reduction in runoff volume, with infiltration gains reported across Indian watershed programmes
indirect gain through retained topsoil and improved biomass production
dry-season refugia support amphibian and invertebrate persistence

source: FAO Soil and Water Conservation practice guidance; ICAR/NABARD watershed development programme reviews

practice: Native hedgerow and field-margin restoration
summary: Converting bare or sprayed field boundaries into multi-species native hedgerows and flowering margins.
mechanism: Fragmented habitat fails mainly because small patches are functionally isolated, not because total area is low. Linear native vegetation reconnects patches, which raises effective population size for species that will not cross open ground. Flowering margins supply nectar through the gaps in crop flowering, so pollinator populations persist rather than crashing between crop cycles, and this carries back into crop pollination service.

effects.magnitude: measurable reduction in effective patch isolation
pollinator and predatory arthropod richness typically among the strongest responders to margin restoration
localised accumulation under permanent woody cover

source: IPBES Global Assessment on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (2019); IPBES Assessment on Pollinators, Pollination and Food Production

practice: Crop rotation with pulses replacing continuous monoculture
summary: Breaking a repeated single-crop cycle with pulses or millets on a two to three year rotation.
mechanism: Continuous monoculture selects for a narrow set of specialist pests and pathogens, which drives pesticide use, which in turn suppresses non-target invertebrates. Rotation breaks the pest cycle biologically rather than chemically, so predator populations recover. Different rooting depths across the rotation also exploit different parts of the soil profile and diversify the carbon inputs feeding soil microbial groups.

effects.magnitude: recovery of natural enemy and soil fauna groups as pesticide pressure falls
modest but consistent gains relative to continuous monoculture
lower pesticide and synthetic nitrogen requirement

source: FAO Save and Grow; IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU)

practice: Mangrove replanting and hydrological reconnection in degraded creeks
summary: Restoring tidal flow to blocked creek sections and replanting site-matched mangrove species rather than a single nursery species.
mechanism: Most failed mangrove plantings fail on hydrology, not on seedlings: without correct tidal inundation frequency the propagules drown or dry. Reconnecting channels first, then matching species to inundation zone, is what produces survival. Restored stands accumulate carbon in waterlogged anoxic sediment where decomposition is slow, which is why mangrove carbon density is among the highest of any ecosystem, and the root structure is nursery habitat for juvenile fish and crustaceans.

effects.magnitude: mangrove systems store several hundred tonnes of carbon per hectare across biomass and sediment, far above terrestrial forest on a per-hectare basis
juvenile fish and crustacean abundance rises sharply once root structure establishes
reconnected creeks restore movement between estuary and intertidal zone

source: FAO/Wetlands International mangrove restoration guidance; IPCC Wetlands Supplement to the 2006 National Greenhouse Gas Inventory Guidelines

practice: Rotational grazing with enforced rest periods
summary: Splitting grazing land into paddocks and moving stock so each paddock gets a defined recovery period.
mechanism: Continuous grazing removes regrowth before the plant has rebuilt root reserves, so root systems shrink and carbon input to soil falls. Rest periods let root mass recover, which is the main pathway by which grassland gains soil carbon. Varying sward height across paddocks also produces structural heterogeneity, and grassland bird and invertebrate richness tracks structural heterogeneity more closely than plant species count.

effects.magnitude: gains reported where stocking rate is also within carrying capacity; overstocking cancels the effect
grassland bird and invertebrate richness responds to sward structural variation
better ground cover lowers runoff and surface crusting

source: FAO Grasslands and Rangelands carbon guidance; IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU)

practice: Farm pond and percolation tank construction
summary: Small excavated storage to capture monsoon runoff for dry-season use and local recharge.
mechanism: In rainfall-limited systems the constraint is usually not annual total but distribution: water arrives in a few intense events and leaves. Capture converts an unusable peak into usable dry-season supply and raises shallow water table locally. Permanent or semi-permanent water is a hard requirement for amphibians and for many invertebrate life cycles, so ponds add a species group the landscape otherwise cannot hold.

effects.magnitude: dry-season irrigation buffer plus local groundwater recharge
amphibian, odonate and waterbird presence where the pond holds water into the dry season
raised shallow water table in the surrounding area

source: FAO water harvesting guidance; NABARD watershed development programme documentation

practice: Riparian buffer strips along watercourses
summary: A vegetated strip of native grasses and trees left uncultivated along stream and drain edges.
mechanism: Buffers intercept surface runoff before it reaches water, so nutrient and sediment load falls. That matters for biodiversity because eutrophication is a dominant driver of freshwater species loss, and reducing load at source is more effective than downstream treatment. The strip simultaneously provides shaded, cool, structurally complex habitat that is disproportionately species-rich relative to its area.

effects.magnitude: large reductions in sediment and nutrient transport to watercourses where buffer width is adequate
freshwater and riparian taxa respond quickly to reduced nutrient load
watercourses become continuous movement corridors

source: IPBES Global Assessment (2019); FAO Water Pollution from Agriculture: a global review

practice: Agricultural liming on acidic soils
summary: Applying agricultural lime or dolomite to raise pH where soil is strongly acidic.
mechanism: Below about pH 5.5 aluminium becomes soluble and toxic to roots, phosphorus is locked in unavailable forms, and the bacterial fraction of soil microbial communities is suppressed relative to fungi. Correcting pH restores nutrient availability and rhizobial function, which is a precondition for legume-based practices working at all. Sequencing matters: liming before sowing legumes avoids wasting the legume intervention.

effects.magnitude: correction toward the 6.0-7.0 range where most nutrients are plant-available
recovery of acid-sensitive soil bacterial and earthworm populations
indirect, through higher biomass production and root input

source: FAO/ITPS Status of the World's Soil Resources; FAO soil acidity management guidance

practice: Gypsum application and organic amendment on sodic or alkaline soils
summary: Gypsum plus organic matter to displace exchangeable sodium where pH is high and structure has collapsed.
mechanism: Sodic soils disperse: clay particles separate, pores seal, and the soil becomes simultaneously waterlogged after rain and hard-set when dry. Calcium from gypsum displaces sodium on the exchange complex and restores aggregate structure, which is what lets water and roots move again. Without structural repair, adding organic matter alone is slow because biological activity is limited by anoxia and mechanical impedance.

effects.magnitude: gradual reduction toward the agronomic range as exchangeable sodium falls
restored infiltration once aggregates re-form
return of soil fauna once anoxia and hardsetting ease

source: FAO/ITPS Status of the World's Soil Resources; FAO salt-affected soils management guidance

practice: Assisted natural regeneration on degraded land
summary: Protecting existing rootstock and natural seedling recruitment instead of clearing and planting nursery stock.
mechanism: Degraded land often retains live root systems and a soil seed bank. Protecting these from fire and grazing produces faster and cheaper recovery than plantation, and the resulting stand is genetically local and structurally mixed rather than even-aged monoculture. Structural and species mixture is what determines whether the recovered vegetation supports a full faunal assemblage rather than just canopy cover.

effects.magnitude: biomass accumulation rates comparable to or above planted equivalents at far lower cost
native assemblage recovery exceeds that of single-species plantation
expansion of existing patches rather than creation of isolated new ones

source: FAO Advancing Assisted Natural Regeneration; IPBES Assessment Report on Land Degradation and Restoration

practice: Residue retention and zero tillage
summary: Leaving crop residue on the surface and drilling the next crop directly instead of ploughing.
mechanism: Tillage physically breaks soil aggregates and exposes protected organic matter to rapid oxidation, and it destroys the fungal hyphal networks and earthworm burrows that structure the soil biologically. Stopping tillage preserves that structure; surface residue then moderates temperature and evaporation. The gain is strongest in the surface layer and can be overstated if deeper horizons are not measured, which is a known caveat in the literature.

effects.magnitude: topsoil gains widely reported, though whole-profile gains are smaller than surface sampling suggests
lower evaporation and better infiltration under residue cover
earthworm and mycorrhizal abundance recover where tillage stops

source: FAO Conservation Agriculture programme; IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU)

practice: Integrated pest management replacing calendar spraying
summary: Threshold-based intervention with monitoring, biological control and selective products instead of scheduled applications.
mechanism: Calendar spraying kills natural enemies along with pests, which removes the biological suppression that would otherwise hold pest populations down, producing dependence on further spraying. Threshold-based intervention keeps enemy populations intact so suppression is partly free. Reduced load also cuts the off-site drift and runoff that drives pollinator and aquatic invertebrate decline.

effects.magnitude: substantial reduction in applied active ingredient where thresholds are followed
natural enemy and pollinator recovery is among the fastest-responding indicators

source: FAO Integrated Pest Management programme; IPBES Assessment on Pollinators, Pollination and Food Production

practice: Mulching with crop residue or biomass
summary: Covering bare soil between plants with residue, straw or pruned biomass.
mechanism: Bare soil in a hot dry climate loses water to direct evaporation and reaches surface temperatures that shut down microbial activity. Mulch cuts both. It is one of the few interventions that changes soil moisture within a single season, which matters when the constraint is water and the landholder cannot wait three years for a structural intervention to work.

effects.magnitude: clear within-season reduction in evaporative loss
gradual surface accumulation as mulch decomposes
detritivore and soil fauna activity rises under stable moist cover

source: FAO Conservation Agriculture and Soil Organic Carbon guidance

practice: Compost and farmyard manure application
summary: Regular application of composted organic matter rather than synthetic nutrients alone.
mechanism: Synthetic nitrogen supplies the nutrient but not the carbon substrate, so microbial biomass stays low and the soil keeps depending on external input. Compost supplies both, and the stabilised fraction resists rapid mineralisation. Raising microbial biomass is the mechanistic step between soil amendment and above-ground biodiversity, because soil fauna abundance drives insectivore food supply.

effects.magnitude: among the most reliable carbon-building interventions where application is sustained
soil microbial and faunal biomass increase
lower synthetic fertiliser requirement and reduced leaching risk

source: FAO/ITPS Status of the World's Soil Resources; FAO Soil Organic Carbon: the hidden potential

practice: Stepping-stone patch planting across fragmented landscapes
summary: Small planted patches placed between larger habitat fragments where a continuous corridor is not feasible.
mechanism: Many species cannot cross a long open gap but can cross a series of short ones. Where land ownership makes a continuous corridor impossible, spaced patches restore functional connectivity at a fraction of the land requirement. Placement matters more than total area: patches must sit inside the dispersal distance of the target species, so the intervention needs a target group defined before planting.

effects.magnitude: functional connectivity restored for species within the relevant dispersal range
recolonisation of isolated fragments by dispersal-limited taxa

source: IPBES Global Assessment (2019); IPBES Assessment Report on Land Degradation and Restoration

practice: Diversified shade canopy in plantation systems
summary: Replacing uniform or absent shade with a mixed native shade canopy over coffee, cocoa, cardamom or similar.
mechanism: Plantation biodiversity value depends almost entirely on canopy structure and species mixture rather than on the crop itself. A mixed native canopy provides vertical stratification, which is the variable most strongly associated with bird and bat richness. Shade also buffers understory temperature, which is increasingly the binding constraint as mean temperatures rise.

effects.magnitude: shade plantations retain a substantial share of adjacent forest bird richness, unlike full-sun systems
above-ground carbon rises with canopy biomass
measurable understory cooling relative to full sun

source: IPBES Global Assessment (2019); FAO agroforestry and biodiversity guidance

practice: Drip irrigation with deficit scheduling
summary: Replacing flood irrigation with drip delivery scheduled against crop water requirement rather than fixed turns.
mechanism: Flood irrigation in semi-arid regions loses a large share to evaporation and deep percolation, and repeated flooding on saline-prone soils raises the water table and mobilises salt. Drip cuts both losses. The biodiversity link is indirect but strong: reduced abstraction leaves more water in the local system, and in over-abstracted basins the surface and shallow groundwater dependent species are the first to go.

effects.magnitude: large reduction in applied water per unit yield relative to flood irrigation
lower salinisation risk where water table rise is avoided
indirect, through reduced pressure on local water bodies

source: FAO Water for Sustainable Food and Agriculture; FAO irrigation efficiency guidance

practice: Fire management and controlled grazing exclusion in regenerating areas
summary: Firebreaks, seasonal grazing exclusion and community fire agreements over areas under regeneration.
mechanism: Regeneration fails most often in the first three years, and the two usual causes are fire and browsing pressure rather than planting failure. Excluding both during establishment is the single highest-leverage low-cost step. It only works if it is socially agreed, which is why fire management is treated as an institutional intervention as much as an ecological one.

effects.magnitude: protects accumulated biomass that fire would otherwise reset
allows fire-sensitive species and slow-establishing woody recruits to persist
retention of litter layer that repeated burning removes

source: FAO Advancing Assisted Natural Regeneration; IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU)

practice: Constructed wetland for agricultural drainage treatment
summary: A shallow vegetated basin intercepting drainage water before it reaches a watercourse.
mechanism: Nutrient removal happens through plant uptake, sediment settling and microbial denitrification in the anoxic root zone. Unlike a buffer strip, a constructed wetland handles channelised drainage that a strip would simply bypass. It also creates permanent shallow water habitat, which in intensively farmed landscapes is usually the scarcest habitat type.

effects.magnitude: high nitrogen and sediment removal efficiency where residence time is adequate
waterbird, amphibian and aquatic invertebrate colonisation
storage buffer during peak flow

source: FAO Water Pollution from Agriculture: a global review; Ramsar Convention wetland restoration guidance

practice: Native species selection over fast-growing exotic monoculture
summary: Choosing site-matched native species mixtures for any planting rather than eucalyptus, acacia or casuarina monoculture.
mechanism: Fast-growing exotic monoculture accumulates carbon quickly and is often chosen for that reason, but it supports a fraction of the faunal assemblage because local herbivores and their predators have no evolutionary relationship with the species. Some fast-growing exotics also draw down shallow groundwater heavily, which in water-limited systems trades a carbon gain for a water loss.

effects.magnitude: native mixtures support substantially higher faunal richness than exotic monoculture at equivalent canopy cover
avoids the heavy groundwater drawdown associated with some fast-growing exotics
native stands function as habitat rather than as a barrier matrix

source: IPBES Assessment Report on Land Degradation and Restoration; FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment

practice: Biochar amendment on degraded low-carbon soils
summary: Incorporating pyrolysed biomass char as a soil amendment alongside organic inputs.
mechanism: Biochar carbon is aromatic and resists microbial breakdown, so it persists in soil far longer than raw organic matter. Its porous structure also holds water and provides microbial habitat. The caveat is that biochar alone adds recalcitrant carbon without much labile substrate, so it performs better combined with compost than on its own, and feedstock and pyrolysis conditions change the result substantially.

effects.magnitude: long-lived carbon addition with residence time measured in decades to centuries
improved water holding capacity, strongest on sandy soils
most biochars are alkaline, so there is a liming side effect to account for

source: IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU) carbon dioxide removal assessment; FAO soil amendment guidance

practice: Multi-species pasture and fodder mixtures
summary: Replacing single-species fodder with grass, legume and forb mixtures.
mechanism: Mixtures root at different depths, which raises total below-ground biomass and extends water capture through the profile. Legume components fix nitrogen, reducing fertiliser need. Flowering forbs in the mixture support pollinators, which a pure grass sward does not, so the same intervention serves fodder yield and pollinator habitat at once.

effects.magnitude: higher root biomass than monoculture sward
pollinator support from flowering forb component
deeper and more complete profile water use

source: FAO Grasslands and Rangelands guidance; IPBES Assessment on Pollinators, Pollination and Food Production

practice: Windbreak and shelterbelt planting
summary: Multi-row tree and shrub barriers planted across the prevailing wind direction.
mechanism: Wind increases evapotranspiration and physically removes fine topsoil, which is the fraction carrying most of the organic matter and nutrients. Shelterbelts reduce wind speed over a downwind distance of roughly ten to twenty times their height, cutting both losses. They are also linear woody habitat, so they contribute to connectivity in the same way hedgerows do.

effects.magnitude: reduced evapotranspiration in the sheltered zone
retention of the wind-erodible fine fraction that carries organic matter
linear woody habitat acting as a corridor

source: FAO agroforestry and windbreak guidance; IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 7 (AFOLU)

practice: Establishing a baseline monitoring protocol before intervention
summary: Fixed sampling points for soil carbon, a repeatable species transect, and dated photo points recorded before any change is made.
mechanism: Without a baseline, improvement cannot be separated from inter-annual variation, and soil carbon in particular varies enough between wet and dry years to mask a real trend for several seasons. This is also the requirement that carbon and biodiversity credit standards impose, so skipping it forecloses later access to those markets regardless of how good the ecological outcome is.

effects.magnitude: enables attribution of change to intervention rather than weather

source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories and 2019 Refinement; Verra and Plan Vivo methodology requirements
